title: Light and seeing
scope: Use your school’s topic list to select the ideas you need. These are original practice questions with illustrative values and suggested self-marking guidance, not official Cambridge papers.

objectives.label: Trace light from a source through an object to the eye.
objectives.note: Draw correct ray-arrow directions and explain seeing a non-luminous object without a seeing beam from the eye.

objectives.label: Explain umbra and penumbra and plan a controlled shadow investigation.
objectives.note: Compare point-like and extended sources; separate the straight-ray approximation from diffraction.

objectives.label: Use the law of reflection to locate plane-mirror images.
objectives.note: Measure angles to the normal, calculate mirror distances, and use backward ray extensions to explain a virtual image.

objectives.label: Explain refraction and state the conditions for total internal reflection.
objectives.note: Link bending to speed changes and incidence angle; distinguish normal incidence and explain apparent depth.

objectives.label: Construct lens ray diagrams and explain image formation in cameras and eyes.
objectives.note: Identify image properties, accommodation and short-sight correction; predict what covering half a lens changes.

objectives.label: Calculate light travel times and explain why distant images show the past.
objectives.note: Use compatible distance and speed units, distinguish one-way from round-trip time, and recognise light-years as distance.

cards.definition: Seeing ordinary objects requires light from them to enter an eye.
cards.explanation: Seeing ordinary objects requires light from them to enter an eye. Looking does not send a seeing beam out of the eye.
cards.example: A lamp can illuminate a book whose reflected light reaches your eyes.
cards.confusion: Looking does not send a seeing beam out of the eye.
cards.question: Explain seeing and distinguish it from a common mistaken idea.
cards.answer: Seeing ordinary objects requires light from them to enter an eye. Looking does not send a seeing beam out of the eye.
cards.cue: Looking does not send a seeing beam out of the eye.

cards.definition: A shadow is a region receiving less light because an object blocks some light paths.
cards.explanation: A shadow is a region receiving less light because an object blocks some light paths. A shadow is not a substance cast out by an object.
cards.example: A broad light source can produce a partial shadow around a darker centre.
cards.confusion: A shadow is not a substance cast out by an object.
cards.question: Explain shadows and distinguish it from a common mistaken idea.
cards.answer: A shadow is a region receiving less light because an object blocks some light paths. A shadow is not a substance cast out by an object.
cards.cue: A shadow is not a substance cast out by an object.

cards.definition: At a reflecting surface, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured to the normal.
cards.explanation: At a reflecting surface, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured to the normal. The normal is perpendicular to the surface, not along it.
cards.example: A ray arriving at 30° to a mirror normal leaves at 30° to that normal.
cards.confusion: The normal is perpendicular to the surface, not along it.
cards.question: Explain reflection and distinguish it from a common mistaken idea.
cards.answer: At a reflecting surface, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured to the normal. The normal is perpendicular to the surface, not along it.
cards.cue: The normal is perpendicular to the surface, not along it.

cards.definition: Light changes propagation direction at a boundary when its speed changes and incidence is oblique.
cards.explanation: Light changes propagation direction at a boundary when its speed changes and incidence is oblique. The change is not because light is attracted towards the normal.
cards.example: An oblique ray entering glass from air usually bends towards the normal.
cards.confusion: The change is not because light is attracted towards the normal.
cards.question: Explain refraction and distinguish it from a common mistaken idea.
cards.answer: Light changes propagation direction at a boundary when its speed changes and incidence is oblique. The change is not because light is attracted towards the normal.
cards.cue: The change is not because light is attracted towards the normal.

cards.definition: A lens refracts light; a converging lens can bring parallel rays towards a focal point.
cards.explanation: A lens refracts light; a converging lens can bring parallel rays towards a focal point. An image need not lose its top half when half a lens is covered.
cards.example: A camera lens forms a real image on a sensor.
cards.confusion: An image need not lose its top half when half a lens is covered.
cards.question: Explain lenses and eyes and distinguish it from a common mistaken idea.
cards.answer: A lens refracts light; a converging lens can bring parallel rays towards a focal point. An image need not lose its top half when half a lens is covered.
cards.cue: An image need not lose its top half when half a lens is covered.

cards.definition: Light travels at a finite speed; in vacuum use c ≈ 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
cards.explanation: Light travels at a finite speed; in vacuum use c ≈ 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. A light-year measures distance, not time.
cards.example: A flash takes a measurable time to cross a very large distance.
cards.confusion: A light-year measures distance, not time.
cards.question: Explain light travel time and distinguish it from a common mistaken idea.
cards.answer: Light travels at a finite speed; in vacuum use c ≈ 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. A light-year measures distance, not time.
cards.cue: A light-year measures distance, not time.

questions.title: Reflection · Worked example
questions.prompt: A light ray meets a plane mirror at 27° to its surface. Calculate the reflection angle measured to the normal.
points: The normal is perpendicular to the mirror: incidence angle = 90° − 27°.
Reflection angle = incidence angle = 63°.
model: The normal is perpendicular to the mirror: incidence angle = 90° − 27°.
Reflection angle = incidence angle = 63°.
accepted: Accept scientifically equivalent explanations and correctly labelled diagrams. Each listed point is worth one suggested mark; do not require identical wording.
questions.common: The normal is perpendicular to the surface, not along it.
hints: At a reflecting surface, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured to the normal.

accepted: Accept scientifically equivalent explanations and correctly labelled diagrams. Each listed point is worth one suggested mark; do not require identical wording.
